## The setup

Take a 0–1 program and its LP relaxation

$$
P = \{\, x : A x \le b,\; 0 \le x \le 1 \,\},
$$

where the bounds $0 \le x \le 1$ are included among the rows of $Ax \le b$. Suppose the LP
optimum $\hat x$ has a fractional binary variable, $0 < \hat x_j < 1$. Every integer
solution satisfies the [split](introduction.qmd)

$$
x_j \le 0 \quad\lor\quad x_j \ge 1 ,
$$

and with the bounds this is the same as $x_j = 0 \lor x_j = 1$. A **lift-and-project cut**
is a cut derived from this disjunction. The name comes from how Balas, Ceria and
Cornuéjols first presented it, as a two-step construction [@balas1993].

## Lift, then project

**Lift.** Multiply every constraint of $P$ by $x_j$, and separately by $(1 - x_j)$. Both
multipliers are nonnegative on $[0,1]$, so the products keep the direction:

$$
(b - A x)\, x_j \ge 0, \qquad (b - A x)(1 - x_j) \ge 0 .
$$

These are quadratic. Make them linear by giving each product its own variable,
$y_i := x_i x_j$. Because $x_j$ is binary, $x_j^2 = x_j$, so set $y_j = x_j$. The
result is a **linear** system in the larger space of $(x, y)$:

$$
b\,x_j - A y \ge 0, \qquad b\,(1 - x_j) - A (x - y) \ge 0, \qquad y_j = x_j .
$$

**Project.** Eliminate $y$ and look at the set of $x$ that remains. Call it $P_j$.

### Why that's the disjunctive hull

Rename the quantities in the lifted system:

$$
\lambda_1 = x_j, \qquad \lambda_0 = 1 - x_j, \qquad v^1 = y, \qquad v^0 = x - y .
$$

The lifted system becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
A v^1 &\le b\, \lambda_1, & v^1_j &= \lambda_1 && (\lambda_1 \times \text{a point of } P \text{ with } x_j = 1), \\
A v^0 &\le b\, \lambda_0, & v^0_j &= 0         && (\lambda_0 \times \text{a point of } P \text{ with } x_j = 0), \\
x &= v^0 + v^1, & \lambda_0 &+ \lambda_1 = 1 .
\end{aligned}
$$

This is exactly the [hull formulation](big-m-vs-hull.qmd) for the disjunction
$x_j = 0 \lor x_j = 1$, with each $v^k$ being "$\lambda_k$ times a point of piece $k$".
So the projection is

$$
P_j \;=\; \mathrm{conv}\Big( \big(P \cap \{x_j = 0\}\big) \,\cup\, \big(P \cap \{x_j = 1\}\big) \Big),
$$

and a lift-and-project cut is any inequality valid for $P_j$ that cuts off $\hat x$
[@balas1993]. In practice you don't build the lifted system and project it. You find the
cut directly with the [cut-generating LP](solving.qmd), using the two pieces
$P \cap \{x_j \le 0\}$ and $P \cap \{x_j \ge 1\}$.

"Lift-and-project" is the historical name for one route to the result. "Disjunctive cut
from a simple binary split" describes the same cut.

## A worked example

Let

$$
P = \{\, x \in [0,1]^2 : 2x_1 + 2x_2 \ge 1 \,\}, \qquad \min\; x_1 + x_2 .
$$

The integer points of $P$ are $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$, so the integer optimum is 1.
The LP relaxation only reaches 0.5. We now run the cutting-plane loop: solve the LP, split
on a fractional variable, solve the CGLP, add the cut, repeat.

| Round | LP optimum $\hat x$ | LP bound | Split | Cut added |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 1 | $(0.00,\, 0.50)$ | 0.500 | $x_2$ | $2\,x_1 + x_2 \geq 1$ |

Walk through it:

1. **Round 1.** The LP optimum is $(0, 0.5)$, so split on $x_2$. The piece with $x_2 = 0$
   is the segment from $(0.5, 0)$ to $(1, 0)$; the piece with $x_2 = 1$ is the top edge.
   Their hull has a new edge from $(0.5, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$, which gives the cut
   $2x_1 + x_2 \ge 1$. It removes $(0, 0.5)$, since $2 \cdot 0 + 0.5 < 1$, and keeps all
   three integer points.
2. **Round 2.** Now the optimum is $(0.5, 0)$; split on $x_1$. With the first cut in
   place, the piece with $x_1 = 0$ shrinks to the single point $(0, 1)$. The hull of that
   point and the right edge is the triangle with corners $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$ —
   **already the integer hull**. But the CGLP returns only *one* inequality valid for that
   triangle, $x_1 + 2x_2 \ge 1$, which cuts off $\hat x$ without being a facet.
3. **Round 3.** The optimum $(1/3, 1/3)$ is still fractional. Another round gives the facet
   $x_1 + x_2 \ge 1$, and the LP now returns the integer point $(0, 1)$ with value 1.

Round 2 shows a general point: a split defines the whole hull $P_j$, but one CGLP solve
returns one cut. Which cut you get depends on the normalization (see the
[CGLP](solving.qmd#the-cut-generating-lp)), so it can take a few rounds on the same
disjunction to recover all of $P_j$.

## Sequential convexification

The example reached the integer hull after splitting on $x_2$ and then on $x_1$ — one
split per binary variable. That isn't luck. For 0–1 programs:

$$
\big(\cdots\big((P_{j_1})_{j_2}\big)\cdots\big)_{j_n} \;=\; \mathrm{conv}\big(P \cap \{0,1\}^n\big),
$$

for any order of the variables. Taking the hull with respect to one binary variable at a
time, each time **starting from the hull already obtained**, gives the integer hull after
$n$ steps. This is Balas's *sequential convexification* for facial disjunctive programs
[@balas1998], and Balas, Ceria and Cornuéjols showed the iterated lift-and-project
procedure is equivalent to it [@balas1993].

It's worth seeing why this is surprising. The integer hull is the hull of a disjunction
with up to $2^n$ terms, one per 0–1 vector. Sequential convexification gets there with
$n$ two-term disjunctions. The catch is that each $P_j$ is described by many
inequalities, so in practice you generate cuts from it a few at a time, as in the example.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why does it work? (the role of "facial")
For a binary variable, the two pieces $P \cap \{x_j = 0\}$ and $P \cap \{x_j = 1\}$ are
**faces** of $P$: each is cut out by an inequality ($x_j \ge 0$ or $x_j \le 1$) that is
valid for all of $P$. Balas calls a disjunctive program *facial* when every disjunction
has this property. For facial programs, convexifying one disjunction never "undoes" the
progress on the others, which is what makes the step-by-step procedure exact
[@balas1998]. General splits like $x_1 + x_2 \le 1 \lor x_1 + x_2 \ge 2$ are usually not
facial, and then the guarantee is lost.
:::

## Two refinements used in practice

**Strengthening.** The CGLP treats every variable other than $x_j$ as continuous. If
other variables are also integer, the cut's coefficients on them can often be tightened
after the fact without losing validity. This is the strengthening procedure of Balas and
Jeroslow [@balasjeroslow1980], which Balas, Ceria and Cornuéjols apply to
lift-and-project cuts [@balas1993].

**The link to Gomory cuts.** Balas and Perregaard showed a precise correspondence between
lift-and-project cuts, simple disjunctive (intersection) cuts, and the mixed-integer
cuts of Gomory [@gomory1960] for 0–1 programs [@balas2003]. In particular, a strengthened lift-and-project cut from
$x_k \le 0 \lor x_k \ge 1$ matches a Gomory mixed-integer cut from a suitable simplex
tableau row. They also used it to solve the CGLP by pivoting in the original LP's tableau
instead of building the larger LP.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Chvátal–Gomory cuts are split cuts too
Let $\pi$ be an integer vector and suppose $\pi^\top x < \pi_0 + 1$ for every $x \in P$.
Then the side $\pi^\top x \ge \pi_0 + 1$ of the split is **empty**, the hull of the union
is just $P \cap \{\pi^\top x \le \pi_0\}$, and the split gives the cut
$\pi^\top x \le \pi_0$. That is exactly a Chvátal–Gomory cut, the cut family that
grew out of Gomory's cutting-plane algorithm [@gomory1958] and Chvátal's closure
[@chvatal1973]. Split cuts were studied in
this generality by Cook, Kannan and Schrijver [@cook1990].
:::
